title: Golden Gate Shoreline
blurb: Fly the Marina waterfront from a Roman ruin to the foot of the bridge.

stops.name: Palace of Fine Arts
stops.line: Welcome to a ruin built on purpose. Maybeck designed this rotunda in 1915 to feel ancient from day one.

stops.name: Wave Organ
stops.line: Listen. At the tip of this jetty the bay itself plays 25 pipes, gurgling louder at high tide.

stops.name: Crissy Field
stops.line: This marsh was an Army airfield. In 1924 a pilot landed here after crossing the country in a single day.

stops.name: Fort Point
stops.line: A Civil War fort that never fired at an enemy. The bridge engineers built an arch just to save it.

stops.name: Golden Gate Bridge
stops.line: International Orange was meant to be primer. Climb above the deck and look back at the whole city.

title: Fisherman's Wharf Waterfront
blurb: Chocolate, Irish coffee, antique arcades, warships and sea lions.

stops.name: Ghirardelli Square
stops.line: A Gold Rush chocolatier's brick factory, saved and turned into one of America's first adaptive reuse projects.

stops.name: The Buena Vista
stops.line: Irish coffee landed in America at this corner bar in 1952. They still pour them in long rows.

stops.name: Musee Mecanique
stops.line: Bring quarters. Laffing Sal has been cackling at visitors since the days of Playland-at-the-Beach.

stops.name: Pier 45 Historic Ships
stops.line: A submarine that rescued 73 prisoners of war. The Liberty ship that sailed back to Normandy in 1994 now docks a short hop east at Pier 35.

stops.name: Boudin Bakery
stops.line: The mother dough here dates to 1849, and Louise Boudin carried it out of the fire in a bucket in 1906.

stops.name: Pier 39 Sea Lions
stops.line: Hear that? The sea lions moved onto these docks in 1990, and the boat owners lost the argument.

title: North Beach and Telegraph Hill
blurb: Focaccia, espresso, Beat poetry and a tower on the hill.

stops.name: Washington Square
stops.line: North Beach's front lawn since 1847. Tai chi at dawn, focaccia at noon, church bells at dusk.

stops.name: Liguria Bakery
stops.line: One product, done perfectly since 1911. When the focaccia sells out, the doors close.

stops.name: Caffe Trieste
stops.line: The first espresso house on the West Coast. Legend says The Godfather was written at a table inside.

stops.name: City Lights and the Beats
stops.line: This bookstore published Howl in 1956 and beat an obscenity charge. The Beats had a headquarters.

stops.name: Coit Tower
stops.line: Lillie Coit chased fire engines and left money to beautify the city. Her tower crowns Telegraph Hill.

stops.name: Filbert Steps
stops.line: Drop down the wooden stairs through Grace Marchant's garden. Listen for the wild parrots.

title: Chinatown Alleys
blurb: Through the Dragon Gate to temples, plazas and fortune cookies.

stops.name: Dragon Gate
stops.line: Step through the gate and you enter the oldest Chinatown in North America.

stops.name: Emperor Norton
stops.line: Emperor Norton, self-crowned ruler of the United States, collapsed near Old St. Mary's here in 1880.

stops.name: Portsmouth Square
stops.line: The original town plaza of Yerba Buena, where the American flag went up in 1846.

stops.name: Waverly Place and Tin How Temple
stops.line: Look up at the painted balconies. Tin How Temple waits three flights above the street.

stops.name: Golden Gate Fortune Cookie Factory
stops.line: Follow the vanilla smell down Ross Alley. Every cookie here is folded by hand.

title: Gold Rush Waterfront
blurb: The Financial District was once the bay. Fly the old shoreline.

stops.name: Ferry Building
stops.line: Before the bridges, everyone arrived right here by boat. The clock tower was the city's front door.

stops.name: Bloody Thursday
stops.line: On Bloody Thursday in 1934, two strikers were killed at this corner. The whole city walked out.

stops.name: Tadich Grill
stops.line: A coffee stand in 1849, California's oldest restaurant today. The fish still hits a mesquite grill.

stops.name: The Buried Ship Niantic
stops.line: You are flying over a buried ship. The Niantic was a hotel until fire took it and landfill swallowed it.

stops.name: Jackson Square
stops.line: Brick survivors of 1906. A whiskey warehouse here famously made it while churches burned.

stops.name: Transamerica Pyramid
stops.line: Protesters wore dunce caps to fight this tower. Now it is the shape everyone draws for San Francisco.

title: Lands End Wilds
blurb: Ruins, shipwrecks and cliffs at the edge of the continent.

stops.name: Sutro Heights
stops.line: Adolph Sutro's garden of 200 plaster statues once covered this bluff. The view is still his.

stops.name: Cliff House
stops.line: There have been several Cliff Houses on this rock. Sutro's grand chateau burned here in 1907.

stops.name: Sutro Baths
stops.line: Seven pools under a glass roof once stood here. Now waves wash through the foundations.

stops.name: USS San Francisco Memorial
stops.line: Real steel from a cruiser's bridge, torn by shells at Guadalcanal, aimed back at the battle site.

stops.name: Lands End Labyrinth
stops.line: A stone labyrinth above the surf. Walk it slowly while the foghorns sound.

stops.name: Legion of Honor
stops.line: A French palace on a cliff, with Rodin's Thinker brooding in the courtyard.

title: Golden Gate Park: Museum Row
blurb: Glasshouses, bandshells, museums and a heron lake.

stops.name: Conservatory of Flowers
stops.line: The oldest building in the park, a Victorian glasshouse that has survived fire, quakes and wind.

stops.name: Spreckels Temple of Music
stops.line: A sugar fortune built this bandshell in 1900. The park band still plays free Sundays.

stops.name: de Young Museum
stops.line: Copper skin, slowly turning green. Its twisting tower gives a free view over the park.

stops.name: California Academy of Sciences
stops.line: A rainforest, an aquarium and a planetarium, all under a roof that is a meadow.

stops.name: Japanese Tea Garden
stops.line: The oldest public Japanese garden in America. Mind the steep drum bridge.

stops.name: Blue Heron Lake
stops.line: Herons have nested on these islands since 1993. The lake took their name in 2024.

title: Golden Gate Park: To the Ocean
blurb: Bluegrass meadows, bison and windmills on the way to the Pacific.

stops.name: Hardly Strictly Bluegrass
stops.line: A banjo-loving banker gave the city a free festival here. The meadow now carries his name.

stops.name: Golden Gate Park Bison
stops.line: Yes, bison. They have grazed in this park since 1891.

stops.name: Dutch Windmill
stops.line: The park was sand, so in 1903 this windmill pumped water to keep it alive.

stops.name: Beach Chalet
stops.line: Step inside for 1930s murals of everyday San Francisco life painted on every wall.

stops.name: Ocean Beach
stops.line: The continent ends here. Do not swim, but do watch the surfers.

title: Mission Murals and Sweets
blurb: The oldest building in town, painted alleys and ice cream on the hill.

stops.name: Mission Dolores
stops.line: Everything in San Francisco is younger than this adobe chapel from 1791.

stops.name: Clarion Alley
stops.line: An outdoor gallery that repaints itself. Over 700 murals have come and gone here.

stops.name: MaestraPeace Mural
stops.line: Seven muralists covered this building in women from across history. Stand back to see it all.

stops.name: Bi-Rite Creamery
stops.line: Salted caramel, hand-made. The line is part of the experience.

stops.name: Dolores Park
stops.line: The city's living room on a sunny day, once a cemetery and a refugee camp.

stops.name: The Golden Fire Hydrant
stops.line: This little hydrant saved the Mission in 1906. Every April 18 it gets a fresh coat of gold.

title: The Great Burrito Debate
blurb: Two legends, one alley of murals and a scoop to settle your stomach.

stops.name: El Farolito
stops.line: Contender one: the super burrito, rice included, eaten long after the bars close.

stops.name: La Taqueria
stops.line: Contender two: no rice, crispy dorado style, crowned best in America. Pick a side.

stops.name: Balmy Alley
stops.line: Walk it off in Balmy Alley, where every garage door has been a mural since the 1970s.

stops.name: Mitchell's Ice Cream
stops.line: Finish with ube or buko at a family scoop shop serving since 1953.

title: Castro to the Haight
blurb: From Harvey Milk's plaza over the hills to the Summer of Love.

stops.name: Harvey Milk and the Castro
stops.line: Harvey Milk ran his campaigns from a camera shop up the street. The rainbow flag flies above his plaza.

stops.name: Castro Theatre
stops.line: A 1922 movie palace with a ceiling built like a tent and a neon sign you can see from blocks away.

stops.name: Vulcan Stairway
stops.line: A street with no road, just garden steps and front doors. The hill picked planet names.

stops.name: Corona Heights
stops.line: Red chert made of ancient plankton skeletons, and one of the best views in town.

stops.name: Buena Vista Park
stops.line: The city's oldest park. Check the gutters for old headstones.

stops.name: Summer of Love
stops.line: Haight and Ashbury, 1967: as many as 100,000 young people arrived with flowers and big ideas.

title: The Summit Circuit
blurb: Climb the city's highest points, from Twin Peaks to the cross on Mount Davidson.

stops.name: Twin Peaks
stops.line: Two summits near the center of the city. Spanish settlers gave them a cheeky name.

stops.name: Sutro Tower
stops.line: 977 feet of steel on three legs. On foggy nights it sails above the clouds.

stops.name: Mount Davidson
stops.line: The real top of San Francisco, about 928 feet, hidden in a fog forest under a cross.

stops.name: Glen Canyon Park
stops.line: Drop into a wild canyon where America's first dynamite factory blew itself up in 1869.

title: Ride the Cable
blurb: Follow the cable cars from the turntable to the bay.

stops.name: Powell and Market Turntable
stops.line: Watch the crew push a cable car around by hand. It is the last system of its kind on Earth.

stops.name: Cable Car Museum
stops.line: The heart of the system. Giant wheels here pull every cable under the streets.

stops.name: First Cable Car
stops.line: On August 2, 1873, the world's first successful cable car started down this hill.

stops.name: Lombard Street
stops.line: The Powell-Hyde car passes the top of these eight famous switchbacks.

stops.name: Powell-Hyde Cable Car
stops.line: End of the line at Hyde and Beach, with the bay spread out below.

title: SoMa Skyline
blurb: Rooftop gardens, sinking towers and modern art in the new downtown.

stops.name: Salesforce Park
stops.line: A park on the roof of a bus station, with a fountain choreographed by buses.

stops.name: Salesforce Tower
stops.line: The tallest building in the city. After dark its crown turns into a giant screen.

stops.name: Millennium Tower
stops.line: The famous leaning tower of San Francisco, sinking into the landfill since 2009.

stops.name: Yerba Buena Gardens
stops.line: A lawn on top of a convention center, with a waterfall memorial to Dr. King.

stops.name: SFMOMA
stops.line: The first West Coast museum for modern art, with a wall that ripples like fog.

title: Civic Center to the Fillmore
blurb: Domes, opera, Victorians and the Harlem of the West.

stops.name: San Francisco City Hall
stops.line: Its dome beats the U.S. Capitol by 42 feet. Joe DiMaggio and Marilyn Monroe married inside.

stops.name: War Memorial Opera House
stops.line: The United Nations was founded at a conference in this opera house in 1945.

stops.name: Painted Ladies
stops.line: Candy-colored Victorians with downtown behind them. Admire from the park.

stops.name: Harlem of the West
stops.line: In the 1950s Coltrane jammed until dawn at Bop City on these blocks.

stops.name: The Fillmore
stops.line: Bill Graham launched the psychedelic rock era here. Grab an apple on the way in.

stops.name: Peace Pagoda
stops.line: A gift from Osaka in 1968, centerpiece of one of America's last three Japantowns.

title: Ballparks and the Bay
blurb: From the Bay Bridge to the stadiums of Mission Bay.

stops.name: Bay Bridge
stops.line: The Bay Bridge beat the Golden Gate by six months and carries far more traffic.

stops.name: Oracle Park
stops.line: Home runs here land in the bay. Watch for kayaks in McCovey Cove.

stops.name: Caltrain at 4th and King
stops.line: The terminal of the oldest continuously operating passenger railroad in the West.

stops.name: Chase Center
stops.line: The Warriors came home across the bay in 2019. On Valkyries nights it is Ballhalla.

title: Sunset Secrets
blurb: Mosaic stairways, a highway turned park and a town of streetcars.

stops.name: Hidden Garden Steps
stops.line: A mosaic garden climbing 148 steps, with a salamander snaking up the middle.

stops.name: 16th Avenue Tiled Steps
stops.line: 163 steps from the sea floor to the stars, tiled by more than 300 neighbors.

stops.name: Carville-by-the-Sea
stops.line: In 1895 retired streetcars became cottages out here in the dunes. This was Carville.

stops.name: Sunset Dunes
stops.line: A four-lane highway until 2025. Now it belongs to skaters, kids and drifting sand.

title: Southwest Cliffs
blurb: A lake, a giant dachshund and the city's soaring hang gliders.

stops.name: Lake Merced
stops.line: One of the city's few natural lakes, where rowers glide across still water at dawn.

stops.name: Doggie Diner Head
stops.line: A seven-foot fiberglass dachshund in a chef's hat, now an official city landmark.

stops.name: Fort Funston Bank Swallows
stops.line: Every hole in these cliffs is a swallow's burrow. One of California's last coastal colonies.

stops.name: Fort Funston Hang Gliders
stops.line: The sea breeze bends up these 200-foot cliffs, and hang gliders ride it for hours.

title: Southeast Shore
blurb: Wetlands, windsurfers and the city's overlooked big park.

stops.name: Heron's Head Park
stops.line: A failed shipping terminal that nature turned into a wetland full of shorebirds.

stops.name: Candlestick Point
stops.line: California's first urban state park, where the famous wind now belongs to windsurfers.

stops.name: McLaren Park
stops.line: The city's fourth-largest park, with an amphitheater named for Jerry Garcia.

stops.name: Mitchell's Ice Cream
stops.line: Reward yourself with a scoop of mango at a family shop serving since 1953.

title: Russian Hill Hideaways
blurb: Ice cream, a storybook lane and the crookedest block.

stops.name: Swensen's Ice Cream
stops.line: The original 1948 parlor of a chain that went worldwide. Its neon still reads The Original Swensen's Since 1948.

stops.name: Macondray Lane
stops.line: The real-life Barbary Lane from Tales of the City, all ferns and wooden steps.

stops.name: Lombard Street
stops.line: Eight switchbacks on one block. Fly the curves without touching a single hedge.

stops.name: House of Prime Rib
stops.line: Since 1949, prime rib carved tableside from gleaming carts. Seconds are on offer.
